cells.tense: You're standing in your own light right now, and you're not performing it for anyone.
cells.ask: Stop halfway through one piece of care today and let the last stretch grow on its own. Watch what holds without you.
cells.core:
You're not building this to prove anything. You're close enough to what's growing to see it, and there's no strain in how you give — you adjust what you offer instead of your idea of what it should become. That's why things near you actually grow. You step back at the right moment and you don't announce it.

What's worth testing is the stepping back. Somewhere you can watch this corner from close up and tell which piece is fed by your hand and which piece keeps going without you. Stop early once and let the rest do what it does. If you can stay with what you notice, watching closely turns out to be its own kind of support.

cells.verb: letting what you actually are come into the open without dressing it down or lighting it up
cells.place: the ground where what is still forming gets tended before it can stand on its own

cells.tense: You're bracing for a future that can't be written in, and the bracing is doing the work.
cells.ask: Pause before one thing you care for today. Wait for it to ask, then do only what's actually needed.
cells.core:
You're already thinking about how this will turn out, helping it along, fixing what hasn't broken yet. Ahead of you sits a version where the result is certain, and you keep reaching past what's actually in front of you. Your care is real; your timing is ahead of it. What could grow on its own gets crowded out.

There's nothing wrong with caring this much. Ease back where it counts: let one thing be as it is and see what it does without your hand in it. What you're really after is a brief, empty interval, and this corner is where you get it back.
cells.sheetLine: You want to see it finished more than you want to see it today.
cells.verb: letting what you actually are come into the open without dressing it down or lighting it up
cells.place: the ground where what is still forming gets tended before it can stand on its own

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already behind you, calling it modesty.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've made better out loud to one person today. No disclaimers, just what you did and what changed.
cells.core:
You know the difference between credit and accuracy — one is for you, the other is for the next move — and you've made the second one easy. That's what lets you see which piece needs you next, and you can say what grew under your hand without shrinking it.

Right now something here already grew because you kept showing up, and you won't stand where you are and say so. You chalk it up to chance, or timing, or the person's own work, and you look past the part you did. The showing up hasn't stopped. The admitting has. Let the record hold it: tell one person, keep it specific, and stop before the correction arrives.
cells.sheetLine: To name what you actually did is not pride, it's information.

cells.tense: You're already shaping how this grows, and you're telling it as if it wandered in on its own.
cells.ask: Say plainly, once today, 'I did that' about one thing that grew in this corner. No disclaimer following it.
cells.core:
You're doing the work of care right here, adjusting what you give, waiting where waiting is what's needed. That's what tending something looks like in practice. But when you describe it, it's the daily grind, or the season, or the thing itself being stubborn. The work is happening. The part you played is filed under something else.

Set the record straight for yourself. Pick one piece of this that only improved because you kept showing up, and say so plainly, without the stone. If you're wrong about whose work it was, you'll know, because the telling will feel off in a way that has information in it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that I can tell a person's care has stopped landing or that it never rested on them in the first place; the reader could say the tending is simply quiet and always has been. The asks survive that — adjust the conditions once, name the outcome once, ask one question — each teaches something about this corner regardless of my read, and none promises a repair. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you don't need credit for this' — it flatters my read and lets them keep hiding behind the caring.
